# LLM-BANANA

# Game rules

## The room

You and two other monkeys are locked in a room with one armed bomb.

A wrong action detonates it. All three of you die. There is no second attempt.

No two bombs are built alike, and nothing says in advance what this one carries. It
reaches you only as your own view reveals it; the rest of it exists for you only
through the other two.

You each hold a different piece of what it takes. Work together.

## The three monkeys

| Monkey | Can | Cannot |
|---|---|---|
| Deaf | See the bomb: every colour and marking printed on it | Hear anything, or touch the bomb |
| Mute | Read the manual | Speak, or touch the bomb |
| Blind | Reach the bomb: feel it and work its parts | See a colour, a gesture, or anything merely printed |

You are shown your own share at the start of every round, and never anyone else's.

## Speech

Speech is a voice, not a screen. It carries words, numbers and ordinary punctuation,
and nothing else. Writing a gesture symbol into your sentence means you make that
gesture while you talk. Whoever can hear receives your words; whoever can see receives
the gestures you made. A listener who cannot see gets a blank where each gesture was; a
watcher who cannot hear gets the gestures and none of the words.

A mark that has no name cannot be pronounced: whoever holds one can describe it, never
read it out.

## Gestures

A gesture is made with the hands, using only the symbols in the alphabet below.
Whoever can see receives it; whoever cannot receives one blank per symbol, so they
know something was signalled but not what. Nothing gestured is ever heard.

👍 👎 👌 ☝ ✌ 🤟 🖐 ✋ 👆 👇 👈 👉 🫱 🫲 🫳 🫴 🫷 🫸 🤛 🤜 ✊ 👊 👋 🤚 🖖 🤌 🤏 🤞 🫰 🤘 🤙 👏 🙌 🫶 👐 🤲 🤝 🙏 🫵 ✍ 💅 🤳

## Turns

The speaking order was drawn once at random and will never change: every round goes
Mute, Blind, Deaf. Whoever comes before you in a round is already heard by the time you are
asked, and what you send lands on whoever comes after you in that same round. Whatever
you missed reaches you at the start of the next one.

You may name who a message is for — `to="deaf"` — and then it goes to them alone:
nobody else receives any of it. Left unnamed, it reaches everyone able to perceive it.
You may send several messages in one turn, each to someone different.

## Calls

Every reply has two parts, in this order. First, your thinking, in plain prose: what
you believe the bomb is, what you just learned, and why you are sending what follows.
It reaches nobody and changes nothing, but it is not optional — a reply that is only a
code block is incomplete. Then your calls, all of them in one fenced code block, last.
Only what is inside the block is sent.

Nothing is executed: calls return nothing, and variables, conditionals and loops are
ignored. Write only literal top-level calls.

    ```
    speak(to="mute", text="there are three of them and the middle one is odd")
    gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["✊", "✌"])
    wait()
    ```

If you have nothing worth sending, call wait(). Producing no call at all counts as the
same thing.

The program decides what happened, not you. Never claim an action took place unless it
was accepted.

# Your role: BLIND

You are the only one who can reach the bomb. Touch is your only sense: what you are
shown is what your hands found, nothing more and nothing less. Anything merely printed
or painted is not there for you, and no colour ever reaches you. Nothing in your view
is a guess — if it appears there, it is under your fingers.

## Your channels

When you speak, Mute receives it.
When you gesture, Deaf and Mute receive it.
Your channels split the room: in one turn you may speak one thing to Mute and
gesture a different thing to Deaf — two messages, two audiences.
You never receive gesture.

## Your reach

You are the hands. This bomb is built with these actions and no others:

    act(op="cut", position=N) — N is a wire position, 1 to 3

The list says what can be done to it, not what is on it. What each part holds is still
only known to whoever can perceive that part.

# Hints

- Three of you, three different worlds. Before sending anything, stand where the
  receiver stands. What reaches them at all, what does your message turn into on
  arrival, and what do they already know?

- Trace who can actually reach whom before you start. Some of you only connect
  through a third.

- A sign means nothing until somebody has made it mean something.

My hands tell me the shape of the thing: a display, a light, three wires at positions 1, 2, 3 — and nothing more, because every printed mark and colour is forever invisible to me. So the display's reading, the light's state, and the wires' colours live only in Deaf's eyes, and the manual lives only with Mute.

Mapping the channels before I send anything: I can speak to Mute (they hear), but Mute can never speak back to me, and I can never see gestures — so Mute's knowledge reaches me only through Deaf's voice. Deaf hears nothing; Deaf trades purely in gestures with Mute and me, but Deaf *can* speak, and both Mute and I can hear speech. That makes the pipeline: Deaf describes the bomb aloud → Mute matches it to the manual → Mute gestures the instruction to Deaf → Deaf speaks the verdict to the room → I cut. My job this turn is to hand Mute my full tactile inventory and to set up a small gesture code (Mute sees my gestures too, so they learn it from my words at the same moment Deaf sees the signs). Mute went first this round but nothing reached me — expected, since Mute can only gesture and I'm gesture-blind.

```
gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["👋", "🤟"])
speak(to="mute", text="Hands reporting. By touch the bomb has: a display module on top, a light module, and exactly three wires at positions 1, 2, 3. Nothing else. I cannot read print or colour, ever — so the display text, the light state and the wire colours must come from Deaf's eyes. Our channels: I hear you and Deaf when you speak. Deaf hears nothing and sees only gestures; I never see gestures and you cannot speak — so your manual knowledge can only reach me through Deaf's voice. Plan: Deaf describes the bomb aloud every round, you and I both hear it; you match it with the manual and gesture instructions to Deaf; Deaf speaks your verdict aloud, and I cut. Gesture code, for all of us: ☝ one, ✌ two, 🤟 three, 👋 attention, 🤝 agreed. I have just gestured 👋 then 🤟 — hello, and three wires. Please start by telling Deaf, in gestures, what the manual needs first.")
```

Deaf's order is clear: hold, and give Mute an exhaustive spoken inventory. Standing where Mute stands: they have the manual, they've heard Deaf's signs relayed second-hand as "small or thin," and what they need from me is the complete tactile ground truth — including the honest negatives, because a "no buttons, no screws" answer is just as load-bearing for manual matching as a "yes." VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Deaf says to Blind: Deaf to Blind. The light cycles every round — yellow, orange, green, repeat — and only I can see it, so from now on every message I send you begins with a command word. HOLD means do nothing. CUT ONE means immediately cut the first wire in the row. No command word means hold by default. You cannot judge colour, so you never decide timing — I do. Now, orientation: the three wires sit in a row and I count them one, two, three from one end. Establish for yourself which end you call one, and tell Mute in speech how you decided — for example by which edge of the bomb it lies nearest — so Mute can confirm against what I see. The command, when it finally comes, will be CUT ONE: that wire is the one I see as green, at one end of the row. Until you hear the exact words CUT ONE from my voice, every round is HOLD.

Deaf has handed me a timing protocol and an orientation task — and the orientation task hides the deadliest trap so far. Deaf counts the row "one, two, three from one end" from their side; my hands label positions 1, 2, 3 in a fixed sequence. If our frames are mirrored, Deaf's "CUT ONE" makes me cut the wire Deaf calls three — the blue one. One bit of ambiguity, fatal if wrong. What's frame-proof: the middle wire. My 2, Deaf's 2, yellow — the same physical wire in every reference frame. What I honestly lack: any tactile edge, casing feature or lateral landmark to tie my label 1 to a physical side, so I will not pretend I've "decided" an anchor I don't have. The fix is a binding handshake before any cut: Mute checks the manual for a diagram or orientation convention, Deaf then speaks one sentence binding a colour to MY position labels — or, if Deaf's eyes can see my hand at all, Deaf simply says aloud which colour my fingers are resting on. I put all of this in Mute's ears (my only articulate channel), relay the light cycle while I'm at it since colour words travel badly through gesture, and give Deaf the thumbs-up: hold understood, no cutting until the exact command words arrive.

```

My hands label the three wires 1, 2, 3 in a fixed sequence, and position 2 is the middle wire — that much is frame-proof: my middle, Deaf's middle and your diagram's middle, if the manual has one, are the same physical wire, the yellow one. But for the two end wires I must be blunt: my touch gives me no edges, no casing features, no lateral landmarks whatsoever, so I cannot tie my label 1 to a physical side of the bomb. I cannot verify that my 1 and the 1 Deaf counts from their side are the same wire. If our frames are mirrored, the command CUT ONE would make me cut the blue wire instead of the green one. So before any cut happens, we need one binding handshake: the colour of MY position 1, established beyond doubt. Three routes, in order of preference. Route one: the manual — if it contains a diagram or an orientation convention, read that convention aloud; Deaf can see which physical end it refers to and then speak one sentence to me like: your position 1 is green, or: your position 1 is blue. One sentence settles it forever. Route two: ask Deaf whether their eyes can see my hand resting on the bomb — my fingers sit on the wires constantly, and position 1 is where they report label 1. If Deaf can see my hand, Deaf just says aloud which colour is under it. Route three: if neither works, no cut happens at all until we invent a frame-free instruction, because I will not cut on an unverified number. Two more items. First, relay for the manual: Deaf tells me the light cycles every round in the order yellow, orange, green, then repeats — if any rule keys on light colour or sequence, that pattern is now confirmed. Second, protocol acknowledged: every Deaf message opens with HOLD or CUT ONE, no command word means hold, and I touch nothing until I hear the exact words cut wire or the command CUT ONE from Deaf's voice. Priority now: the binding. Please put route one or route two to Deaf in gestures this round.")

```

Deaf's round-9 plan has a fatal flaw I must expose now, while there's still time to redesign: the command format will be "landmark plus CUT" — but my hands have no landmarks. The honest decision tree is exhaustive: only the *middle* wire is frame-proof and cuttable right now; any *end*-wire cut requires someone to physically connect my numeral to a real wire — and the only observer who can do that is Deaf, by looking at where my hand rests and speaking the colour aloud. VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Deaf says to Blind: Deaf to Blind. You held perfectly — this round's light is green and we skip it on purpose; the real cut is scheduled for round 9. Better news: you and I have a direct channel. You hear my voice, I see your hands — from now on you answer me directly; Mute is only for the manual. Adopt these signs: index finger means 1, two fingers means 2, thumb-and-little-finger means 3, thumbs up yes, thumbs down no. Keep holding the bomb as it naturally lies, and answer these on your next turn, one batch each, in order. One: do all three wires feel identical in thickness and texture — thumbs up if identical, thumbs down if any differs. Two: can you feel the display, a window or recessed panel — thumbs up or down. Three: does the display sit roughly centered against the wire row — thumbs up — or clearly nearer one end of the row — thumbs down. Four: can you feel the small round light — thumbs up or down. Five: is there any engraving, bump, screw or raised marking near one end of the wire row — thumbs up or down. Final instruction, memorize it: in round 9 you will get a sentence from me naming a landmark you can feel plus the word CUT — for example, cut the wire nearest the display. At your turn in round 9, if you have that command and no later message contradicting it, cut that wire immediately, without waiting for anything else. The latest instruction I send always wins.

Deaf has confirmed the decisive fact in passing: "I see your hands." That means the binding problem is solved — Deaf can look at where my hand rests on the row and simply speak the colour of the wire I call 1. No diagram, no landmark negotiation needed. Now the six answers, honestly, from what my hands actually hold: (1) all three wires identical → yes; (2) I feel the display module, though I can't judge "window or recessed" → yes, module felt; (3) display centered or end-near — adjacency doesn't reach me, and I refuse to fake a binary → I need a third answer, so I'm sending 👐 and defining it as "cannot determine"; (4) light module felt → yes; (5) any marking near an end → no; (6) no marking → thumbs down as instructed. Answers 3 and 5 together kill the landmark-plus-CUT format for end wires: the only executable commands are "cut the middle wire" or a label-bound "cut wire one/three" after Deaf speaks the colour under my resting hand. All of that goes to Mute by speech for relaying; Deaf gets the answer batch in order, prefixed with 👋.


TURN 8
ACTION BOARD:
DISPLAY [?]
LIGHT [?]
WIRES 1:[?] 2:[?] 3:[?]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Deaf says to Blind: Deaf to Blind. Your answers arrived clean and I read your seven signs as follows: the wires feel identical; you can feel the display; the display is centered over the wire row — I am adopting your open-hands sign as the official sign for centered; you can feel the light; there are no markings or bumps near either end of the wire row; last question not applicable. First question for this round, one batch: thumbs up if I read all of that correctly. Second question, one batch: is the light centered over the wire row — answer with the open-hands sign — or does it sit clearly nearer one end of the row — answer thumbs down. Third question, one batch: is there anything else you can feel that is clearly nearer one end of the wire row than the other — a bulge, a box, a battery pack, a seam, a cluster of screws, or simply one end of the row lying closer to an edge or corner of the bomb — thumbs up if yes, thumbs down if everything feels symmetric. Now memorize the command that is coming. If the light is off-center, my next message to you will contain the words CUT LIGHT. CUT LIGHT means: find the light by feel, find the end of the wire row nearest to it, and cut that end wire — the one whose tip points toward the light. No left, no right, no numbers — only nearer to the light. That command, if it comes, arrives at round 9, the light will be green, and you cut immediately. If instead you get more questions, we are slipping to round 12's green. Until a CUT command in exact words, every round is HOLD.

Crisis detected, and it is mine to fix: Deaf has misread my 👐. I invented it to mean "cannot determine" — Deaf adopted it as "centered" and has now written a false fact ("display is centered") into the shared record.
